title: Tree Traversals (DFS & BFS)
tagline: Pre/in/post-order DFS and level-order BFS — the four ways to visit every node.

intuition.analogy: Exploring a building: DFS is one person walking as deep as possible down a corridor before backtracking; BFS is sweeping floor by floor, checking every room on a level before going downstairs.
paragraphs: Every tree algorithm starts with traversal — a systematic way to visit all nodes. Depth-first search (DFS) plunges down one branch fully before exploring siblings; breadth-first search (BFS) fans out level by level.

DFS has three flavours that differ only in WHEN you 'visit' the current node relative to its children: pre-order (node, then children), in-order (left, node, right — which yields sorted order in a BST), and post-order (children, then node — needed when a node's result depends on its subtrees).
BFS uses a queue and naturally computes shortest distances in terms of edges, making it the tool for 'level' problems, minimum depth, and width.
intuition.keyIdea: DFS = recursion/stack (depth first); BFS = queue (level by level). The visit timing defines pre/in/post-order.

steps.title: DFS recursion
steps.detail: dfs(node): if null return; the relative position of 'visit(node)' among the two recursive calls chooses pre/in/post-order.

steps.title: Iterative DFS
steps.detail: Use an explicit stack to avoid recursion limits. Push children in reverse so the left child is processed first.

steps.title: BFS with a queue
steps.detail: Enqueue the root; repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it, and enqueue its children. Process one level fully before the next.

complexity.timeReason: Each node and edge is processed exactly once.
complexity.space: O(h) for DFS (recursion depth = tree height), O(n) worst case
complexity.spaceReason: BFS queue can hold an entire level (up to n/2 nodes); DFS stack is the height h.

pitfalls: Recursive DFS can stack-overflow on skewed (linked-list-like) trees of depth n.
In-order on a BST is sorted — a frequent 'gotcha' that turns hard problems easy.
Mixing up child push order in iterative DFS reverses the visit order.

dryRun.clickMoment: Compare pre-order and post-order: the root is first in one and last in the other. Post-order is exactly what you want when a node's answer needs both subtree answers first — like computing heights or sums.

problems.title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
problems.statement: Return the in-order traversal of a binary tree.
problems.hint: Recursion, or an explicit stack pushing left spines.

approach: Inorder = left, node, right. Iteratively push all left descendants, then pop to visit and move to the right child.
A stack replaces recursion; each node is pushed and popped once.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.statement: Return node values grouped by level.
problems.hint: BFS, capturing the queue size to delimit each level.

approach: Breadth-first with a queue. Process one full level at a time by capturing the queue's size before the loop.
Append each level's values as a sub-list.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.statement: Check whether a tree is a valid BST.
problems.hint: In-order traversal must be strictly increasing.

approach: A BST is valid iff an inorder traversal is strictly increasing, or equivalently every node lies within a (low, high) bound inherited from ancestors.
Recurse passing tightened bounds: left child must be < node, right child > node.

problems.title: Construct Tree from Preorder and Inorder
problems.statement: Rebuild a binary tree from its pre-order and in-order arrays.
problems.hint: Pre-order gives the root; in-order splits left/right subtrees.

approach: The first preorder element is the root; its position in inorder splits left and right subtrees.
Use a hash map of value→inorder index and a moving preorder pointer to build the tree recursively in O(n).

problems.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problems.statement: Return the values visible from the right side.
problems.hint: BFS and take the last node per level (or DFS visiting right first).

approach: The right side view is the last node seen at each level in a BFS.
Do level-order traversal and record the final node of every level. (A right-first DFS tracking depth also works.)
